items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-01-10
items.q: I played Duke Ellington, I played Count, I played Dizzy Gillespie, I played it all.

ctx.x: Well, well, did you, I know you probably did, and there's a whole article in the Jazz Archivist. Yeah. And we're talking about New Orleans in the 60s, and they're talking about, a lot of it about the modern jazz scene. Did you follow the pop, the bebop scene in New Orleans?

Well, you know, really, if you think about it, uh, if you think about it, when I first went on the end, uh, my, uh, theme song was Blue Flame by Woody Herman. And a lot of people say, well, here's a black dance jockey playing black, white music, but hell, I was a lover of the music that Woody Herman played, and Stan Kenton played, and the rest of the guys, you know, I played white, I played Duke Ellington, I played Count, I played Dizzy Gillespie, I played it all. In fact, I was more of a jazz, a jazz disc…
What about, uh, what about the, like, Miles Davis?

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1995-08-29
items.q: The three black newspapers we had... showed pictures of Conk Basie... Sure. But they had never seen these people. They've only rarely heard them.

ctx.x: All right, well. I'm sorry. Let me ask a question. I had a broader question I was going to get back to WMR. Why do you think, finally, at this point in time, that there is black radio, finally? All right.

All right. You've got to remember. Now, we started talking about the black newspapers. The three black newspapers we had, the Informer Sentinel, La Courier, and Louisiana Wheeler, showed pictures of Conk Basie, Duke Ellington, Jimmy Liggins, Billy Eckstein, Joe Lewis. Image factors that blacks could look up to. Sure. But they had never seen these people. They've only rarely heard them. See, you didn't have jukeboxes. You had jukeboxes, but they were just beginning to highlight the black intelligentsia and…
But you met a lot of women, huh, Tex?

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1995-07-21
items.q: And then Count Basie came up with going to Chicago with his big time band. I wanted to go to Chicago.

ctx.x: So, tell us what a Zoot Suit is for somebody who doesn't know what a Zoot Suit is.

Well, now, let me tell you what a Zoot Suit is. In 1939, Clark Gable came out with Gone with the Wind and everybody's wearing these long coats. Kev Calloway got on radio, I mean on the movies, and he started with his hidey hole thing with the big white, big apple hat and with the Zoot Suit and it started taking off. The image factor. And then Count Basie came up with going to Chicago with his big time band. I wanted to go to Chicago. I finally got to Chicago, but before I got to Chicago, I wanted to make sure…
Was that about why you bought the Zoot Suit?

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-08-23
items.q: August Jackson... brought in Count Basie.

ctx.x: Because this was what you would call spiritual rejuvenation. A lot of people didn't understand what was happening with the blues, especially some of the white bands who just started picking up on the blues into the late 80s, that the blues really came out of the black church. And, well, prior to that, the sacrifices that blacks made were harmed from the soul because they paid so many dues. And then, as I talked with my old great uncles from way back when they spoke with their ancestors and relatives during the…
Did that cause the demise of that club? Because I don't think it...
